text.p: A run-up in copper prices finally stalled on Friday and prices ended weaker despite a drop in stocks on the London Metal Exchange to a six-year low.

Oil prices also eased, reversing course after recent strength as traders took profits ahead of the weekend and this week's OPEC meeting in Vienna, while gold remained under pressure on weak fundamentals.
The Commodity Research Bureau Index of 17 futures contracts fell 1.49 points to 244.19 points.
METALS - Base metals fell back from their earlier highs by the LME close on Friday although traders said this was mainly due to end-week profit-taking and light broker liquidation.
Aluminium slipped from its earlier 3-1/2 month high of $1,535 a tonne, while copper drifted towards $2,200.
A tight physical market, recent investment fund buying and uptrending charts helped to underpin the aluminium market.

"Although it's below its highs aluminium has performed well on the upside, a move that may encourge fresh short-covering next week," one trader said. Three months delivery aluminium was last at $1,530, against Thursday's $1,504 close.
Traders said aluminium's performance reflected investment fund shorts following forward selling last October.
They said a large proportion of aluminium stocks are tied up in long term financing deals and are not readily available to the market to alleviate the growing tightness.
A break above resistance at $1,540 next week could spark a move towards $1,600, some traders said.
"No one is likely to run the market short at the moment," one said. He said there could be fresh consumer buying soon.

Copper dipped from a high of $2,218 to settle at $2,208, down $4. Overall the copper market remained quiet and continued to consolidate. Traders will watch closely the LME stocks data next week on Tuesday and Friday. Several are expecting inventories to rise after a long string of declines.
Nickel snapped higher on the back of buy-stops and despite an LME stocks rise. It was last at $6,910, a gain of $40.

But given nickel's recent poor chart performance, which saw prices down to a two-year low of $6,650 last week, several traders expect further downside pressure. Other metals were quiet. Zinc rose $4 to $1,080 and lead was down $3 at $710.

GOLD - Precious metals futures ended lower again in New York on Friday with gold barely holding above its 20-month low posted Thursday. "The partial recovery early this month enabled some funds to lighten up short positions, but everybody's back in now, with a target of $370 for spot gold," said Jeff Singer, Imperial Bank's chief dealer in California. "Gold's fundamentals have been bearish for long time and are probably already discounted into current prices, but things could really get interesting if $370 breaks," he said. OIL - Oil markets were weaker in New York, reversing course after recent strength as traders took profits ahead of the weekend and next week's OPEC meeting in Vienna. January crude ended 9 cents lower at $23.75 a barrel. Participants began to be less worried about forecasts of colder weather over the next week on reports that diplomats saw some momentum picking up toward implementing the Iraq-United Nations oil-for-food deal.

Under the deal, sanctions would be lifted by the United Nations against Iraq, allowing Iraq to sell $2 billion worth of oil in exchange for humanitarian aid. With the Organisation of Petroleum Producing Countries meeting in Vienna next week, traders said the market could continue to be volatile.

"The seesaw market is going to continue next week due to these political crosscurrents," said Ritterbusch. A rollover of OPEC's self-imposed but widely ignored 25.03 million barrel per day production ceiling is expected by many traders.

GRAINS - CBOT December wheat closed up on tight domestic stocks and technicals, while other months closed mixed, traders said. Wheat closed two cents higher to two cents lower, with December up two at $4.10-1/4.
